setup.zh: 正殿里没有神像，只有一口空的石座，四方，四足。石座前立着测灵石，观主玄沉子坐在一旁。轮到你了。
setup.en: No statue in the main hall — only an empty stone seat, square, on four feet. Before it stands the spirit stone; the abbot Xuanchenzi sits beside it. It is your turn.

recap.zh: 测灵石测出了你的灵根；瞿老说「腿稳，心细」，观主说：收，外门。
recap.en: The spirit stone read your roots; Elder Qu said "steady legs, careful heart," and the abbot said: take them — the outer court.

zh: 正殿没有神像，只有一口空的石座。
四方，四足，大得能躺下一个人。
测灵石前，把手放上去——看它亮几种颜色。
en: No statue in the hall — only an empty stone seat.
Square, four-footed, big enough to lie in.
Before the spirit stone: lay your hand on it, and see how many colours it shows.

text.zh: 石面正中一块颜色比别处深，四四方方，仿佛许多年前，那上头曾经压过一样很重很重的东西。
text.en: In the middle of the stone top is a patch darker than the rest, square, as if many years ago something very, very heavy had once pressed down on it.

text.zh: 石面光溜溜的，正中凹下去一块，是千百只手按出来的。你把手心在衣襟上擦了两擦。
text.en: The stone is worn smooth, a hollow pressed into its middle by a thousand hands. You wipe your palm twice on your coat.

text.zh: 那扫地的老头不知什么时候也进了殿，拄着扫帚，靠在门框上，谁也不看。
text.en: Somehow the old sweeper has come into the hall too; he leans on his broom against the doorframe and looks at no one.

story.zh:
正殿在山门里头最高的一层台子上。殿很大，很旧，梁上的彩画褪得只剩了影子，殿里没有神像，只在正中间，摆着一口空的石座。那石座四四方方，底下四只脚，大得能躺下一个人，石面正中一块颜色比别处深，四四方方，仿佛许多年前，那上头曾经压过一样很重很重的东西。石座前头，立着一块一人多高的测灵石，灰不溜秋，看不出什么稀奇。石座旁边一张蒲团上，坐着观主，一身灰袍，面目温和，看上去比山下镇上卖布的掌柜还要和气几分。那扫地的老头不知什么时候也进了殿，拄着扫帚，靠在门框上。

过了三试的孩子，统共一百来个，在殿里排成长长的一队。小满排在最后，只马小宝一个是滑竿抬上来的，排在他后头。唱名的，还是早上石阶底下那个执事，靠在柱子上。

有孩子问这石座是做什么的，为什么不供神仙，唱名执事道：「给鼎留的。三百年了。」

执事拿下巴指一指测灵石，照例背规矩：「手按上去。石头照你身上的五行亮：金白，木青，水黑，火红，土黄。亮一种颜色的，单灵根，又叫天灵根，上上之资——本观三百年，没测出过一个。天灵根的孩子，还在襁褓里，便叫大宗门拿银子抱走了，轮不到泗水边上来爬台阶。」一个孩子问：「襁褓里的娃娃，话都不会说，怎么看得出来？」执事眼皮也不抬：「《抱朴子》上写着：『诸得仙者，皆其受命偶值神仙之气，自然所禀。故胞胎之中，已含通道之性。』娘胎里带来的，石头不过照一照。」

殿里没有人笑这一句。小满看着那张没睡醒的脸。他想起河滩上那一片青，想起那一声「哥——」。娘胎里带来的，石头照一照，银子一放，人便抱走了。原来这是规矩，规矩还写在书上。

执事接着背：「亮两种，双灵根，上中；亮三种，三灵根，中上——这两样，都叫真灵根。亮四种、五种的，叫伪灵根：四种，下中；五种都亮的——」他拖长了声音，「下下。颜色越少、越亮，越好。还有一样，石头不亮颜色，起一阵风、打一个闪、结一层霜的，叫异灵根，比天灵根还少，本观没见过。今年外门，收一百零八个。测完了，玄沉子观主点头，便是收。」他提着笔，在名册上一个一个地数，收一个，划一笔。数到中间，笔尖在一行上滑了过去，没停，那一行底下是四个新写的字。

队伍一寸一寸地往前挪。前头每亮一回石头，殿里便响一回：亮得好的，一片惊叹；亮得暗的，一片笑。昨夜廊下那个光脚的孩子排在前头，脚底板上的草叶子还没摘，一按，亮了四种颜色，「下中」。他咧开嘴，回头冲人堆里竖起一根指头。执事照例问生辰，他张口报了一个年份——石阶底下他报的是十二——报完了，脸一下子白了。执事掐着指头一算：「十一。告示上写的，十二起。」那孩子道：「过了年就十二！」执事道：「过了年，再过三年，下回开山门，你再来。」观主看了他一会儿，没有点头。那孩子没哭，走到殿角，攥着他那块三道画满的考牌，站着。

小满一面挪，一面数：前头还有三十一个人，名册上还剩三十二个名额——够，连他，刚刚够。挪到前头剩二十个的时候，身后一挤，马家的家丁把马小宝塞到了他前头。小满又数了一遍：前头二十一个，名额二十一个。他自己，是第二十二个。孙二狗排在小满前头不远，回过头来冲他咧了咧嘴，小声道：「三步一口气。」二试他是把五搁在了中间，「因为五在一到九的正当中，跟饭碗搁在桌子正当中一个道理」，老执事听了半天，说道理不对，意思对了，给他画了一道；三试他是闭着眼睛冲进去的，冲到古松底下，一头撞在树上，撞出一个包，算是摸过了。

轮到孙二狗了。他把手放上去，测灵石半天没有动静，好一会儿，才极勉强地透出一点光来，四种颜色，淡得像隔着一层窗户纸。唱名的执事还当是石头坏了，伸手在石头上拍了两下，那光也不见亮。执事叹了口气，念道：「金、木、火、土，四门，伪灵根，色又极淡。下下之资。」殿里有人笑。孙二狗没有笑，也没有低头，只把那个比他身子还大的包袱，往背上紧了紧。那包袱里装的，是他娘给他缝的三双鞋，一双比一双大，是预备着他在山上一年一年地长个子的。观主看了他一会儿，点了点头。执事划了一笔。

排在小满前面第三个的，是阿禾。她把两根小辫子往肩后一甩，把手放上去，测灵石亮起三种颜色，青、黑、黄，亮得刺眼。执事一下子睁开了没睡醒的眼睛，念道：「木、水、土，三灵根——真灵根。中上之资。」殿里一阵惊叹。小满张了张嘴，满殿的人，到底没敢喊出声来。

轮到马小宝了。执事看了一眼名册，道：「一百零七。还剩一个。」马小宝把手往测灵石上一拍，拍得「啪」的一声，好像拍的是自家的桌子。测灵石亮了，金白、红、黄三种颜色，却发浑，像蒙了一层灰。执事念道：「金、火、土，三灵根，色浊。中下之资。」他伸手要过马小宝的考牌，一看，一道，一个圈，还空着一格，眉头便皱了起来。马小宝身后那个家丁凑上前，把那封荐书又亮了一亮。执事看看荐书上的落款——那落款，他是认得的——又看看观主。观主没有说话。执事便提起笔来，在那空着的一格里，自己添了一道，道：「荐书在，这一格，算补过了。」又在名册上写了个字，把最后那一格划掉了：「一百零八。名额满了。后头的，不用测了。」

后头只剩小满一个。他没有走。他在心里算：不测，考牌上三道，就是三道白画；测了，就算不取，名册上也有他沈小满一行。他道：「执事，我三道画满了。我测。」执事看了看他手里的考牌，拿下巴一指：「测吧。测完了下山。」

他往前走的时候，心里那块石头又压了上来——不是名额，是眼前这块测灵石。它测的是人身上的灵气；那他胸口木牌里睡着的那个，算不算他身上的？要是这石头一亮，亮出一道银光来，亮出一条尾巴来，满殿的人都瞧见了——「藏。在你打得过所有人之前，不许让任何人知道本王。」小满的手心里，登时出了一层冷汗。他隔着衣裳，把那块木牌往怀里按了按。木牌凉凉的，一动不动，凉得像一块真正的木头。那不是她睡得沉，是她把自己藏起来了，藏得比他还好。

他把手放在测灵石上。
story.en:
The main hall stood on the highest terrace inside the gate. It was large and old, the paintings on its beams faded to shadows; there was no statue in it, only, in the very middle, an empty stone stand. The stand was square, four feet beneath, big enough for a man to lie on, and in the middle of its top was a patch darker than the rest, square, as if many years ago something very, very heavy had once pressed there. In front of it stood a spirit-testing stone taller than a man, dusty grey, nothing remarkable to look at. On a cushion beside the stand sat the abbot, in a grey robe, his face mild, looking even kinder than a cloth merchant in the town below. The old sweeper had come into the hall too, no one knew when, leaning on his broom in the doorway.

The children who had passed all three trials, a hundred or so in all, lined up in a long queue in the hall. Xiaoman was last, with only Ma Xiaobao, carried up in his chair, behind him. Calling the names was the same steward who had called them that morning at the foot of the stair, the face that had never quite woken up, leaning against a pillar.

A child asked what the stone stand was for and why it held no god; the roll-calling steward said, "Kept for a *ding*. Three hundred years now."

The steward pointed his chin at the testing stone, and recited the rules as usual: "Hand on it. The stone lights by the five elements in you: metal white-gold, wood green, water black, fire red, earth yellow. One colour: a single root, also called a heavenly root, the highest of the high — this temple hasn't tested one in three hundred years. Heavenly-root children are carried off in swaddling clothes by the great sects, for silver; they never get as far as climbing stairs by the Si." A child asked: "A baby in swaddling clothes can't even talk — how can anyone tell?" The steward didn't lift his eyelids. "It's written in the *Baopuzi*: 'All who attain immortality met the breath of the immortals at the moment their fate was given — it is what they were born with. So even in the womb they already carry a nature that leads to the Way.' Born with it; the stone only shows it."

No one in the hall laughed at that. Xiaoman looked at the face that had never quite woken. He thought of that sheet of green on the flats, of that cry, "Brother —". Born with it; a stone shows it; silver is set down, and the child is carried off. So this was the rule, and the rule was written in a book.

The steward went on reciting: "Two colours, a double root, above the middle; three, a triple root, just above the middle — both of those are called true roots. Four or five colours are false roots: four, below the middle; all five lit —" he drew it out, "— the lowest of the low. The fewer the colours and the brighter, the better. And one more kind: the stone shows no colour but raises a gust, a flash, a skin of frost — a variant root, rarer than a heavenly one; this temple has never seen one. This year the outer court takes a hundred and eight. When you're tested and Abbot Xuanchenzi nods, you're in." Brush in hand, he counted down the register one by one, a stroke for each taken. Halfway down, the brush slid over one line without stopping; under that line were four freshly written words.

The queue crept forward inch by inch. Each time the stone lit up front, the hall made a noise: a bright one, a gasp; a dim one, a laugh. The barefoot boy from last night's veranda was ahead in the line, grass leaves still under his soles; he pressed, and four colours lit — "below the middle". He grinned and held up one finger to the crowd behind him. The steward asked his birth date as usual; he blurted out a year — at the foot of the stair he'd said twelve — and as soon as it was out his face went white. The steward counted on his fingers. "Eleven. The notice says twelve and up." The boy said, "Twelve after New Year!" The steward said, "After New Year, and three years after that, the next time the gate opens — come back then." The abbot looked at him a while, and didn't nod. The boy didn't cry. He went and stood in a corner of the hall, gripping his tag with its three full strokes.

Xiaoman counted as he shuffled: thirty-one people ahead, thirty-two places left in the register — enough; counting himself, just enough. When the ones ahead were down to twenty, there was a shove from behind, and the Ma servants squeezed Ma Xiaobao in ahead of him. Xiaoman counted again: twenty-one ahead, twenty-one places. He himself was the twenty-second. Sun Ergou, not far ahead, turned and grinned at him. "Three steps, one breath," he whispered. In the second trial he'd put the five in the middle "because five is right in the middle of one to nine, same as you put the rice bowl right in the middle of the table"; the old steward listened a long while, said the reasoning was wrong but the idea was right, and gave him a stroke. In the third he'd charged in with his eyes shut, run head first into the pine, raised a lump, and that counted as touching it.

Sun Ergou's turn. He laid his hand on it, and for a long while the stone did nothing; then, very grudgingly, a little light seeped out, four colours, faint as if seen through window paper. The name-calling steward thought the stone had broken and slapped it twice; the light got no brighter. The steward sighed and read: "Metal, wood, fire, earth — four, a false root, and very faint besides. The lowest of the low." Someone in the hall laughed. Sun Ergou didn't laugh, and didn't lower his head either; he only hitched the bundle bigger than himself higher on his back. In it were three pairs of shoes his mother had sewn, each bigger than the last, for him to grow into year by year on the mountain. The abbot looked at him a while, and nodded. The steward made a stroke.

Third in line ahead of Xiaoman was Ahe. She flicked her two little braids back over her shoulders, laid her hand on it, and the stone lit three colours, green, black, yellow, dazzling. The steward's sleepy eyes flew open. "Wood, water, earth — three roots — a true root. Just above the middle." A gasp went round the hall. Xiaoman opened his mouth — with the whole hall there, he didn't dare call out after all.

Then it was Ma Xiaobao's turn. The steward looked at the register. "A hundred and seven. One left." Ma Xiaobao slapped his hand on the stone — *smack* — as if it were his own family's table. The stone lit: white-gold, red and yellow, but dingy, as if under a film of dust. The steward read: "Metal, fire, earth — three roots, muddy. Below the middle of the middle." He held out his hand for Ma Xiaobao's tag, looked — one stroke, one circle, one square still empty — and frowned. The servant behind Ma Xiaobao stepped up and showed the letter of recommendation once more. The steward looked at the signature on the letter — a signature he knew — then at the abbot. The abbot said nothing. So the steward took up his brush and added a stroke in the empty square himself. "The letter stands; this square counts as made up." Then he wrote a word in the register and struck out the last place. "A hundred and eight. Places full. The rest needn't be tested."

Only Xiaoman was left behind. He didn't go. He reckoned: not tested, three strokes on his tag were three strokes for nothing; tested, even if not taken, the register would have a line with Shen Xiaoman on it. He said: "Steward, my three strokes are full. I'll be tested." The steward looked at the tag in his hand and pointed his chin. "Go on then. Then go down the mountain."

As he stepped forward the stone in his heart pressed down again — not the places now, but this testing stone in front of him. It tested the spirit qi in a person; then the one asleep in the token on his chest — did she count as his? If the stone lit and showed a streak of silver, showed a tail, and the whole hall saw — "Hide. Until you can beat everyone, no one is to know of me." A layer of cold sweat broke out on Xiaoman's palms. Through his clothes he pressed the token closer to his chest. It was cold and perfectly still, as cold as a real piece of wood. It wasn't that she was sleeping deeply; she had hidden herself, hidden better than he could.

He laid his hand on the testing stone.

label.en: Give your birthday · The root test

exits.means: gives the day they were born, or lets the stone read them — the page card asks it

story.zh:
测灵石亮了——亮得很暗。

金白、青、黑、红、黄，五种颜色，一样不少，都有一点，哪一种都不多，哪一种都不亮，你挤着我，我挨着你，灰蒙蒙地搅在一处，像他娘拿家里用剩下的五种碎布头，拼成的一块抹布。{主亮}

殿里静了一静。

然后，有人笑出了声。笑得最响的，是马小宝。他笑得前仰后合，笑得手里的桂花糕渣子掉了一地，拿手指着那块测灵石，如同指着一个天大的笑话。他这一笑，殿里的孩子们便都笑了，一个传一个，一片一片地笑开去，笑声撞在那褪了色的大梁上，又落下来。

唱名的执事也笑了一笑，拖长了声音念道：「金、木、水、火、土——五行俱全。五门俱全的伪灵根，外门叫杂灵根。下下之资。」他提起笔来，「名额已满。不取。」

笔尖朝名册上「不取」那一栏落下去。小满站在测灵石跟前，手还放在石头上，没有拿下来。三百级是他自己走上来的，洛书是他自己算出来的，蠪侄的真头是他自己听出来的——到头来，一块石头，一支笔。他想起舅舅在一百六十级上坐下的那一炷香，想起林子口草地上那件盖着的破袄。满殿的人，笑的笑，看的看，只有两个人没有笑：一个是蒲团上的观主；另一个是阿禾。她站在人堆后头，低着头，拿炭条在本子上记了一笔，记得很重，炭条都记断了。

小满在心里飞快地算了一笔账：不说，是出去；说了，最多也是出去。他把手从测灵石上拿下来，从怀里摸出那块考牌，举了起来，道：「执事。」殿里的笑声小了一些。他道：「今天早上，石阶顶上那位老人家说，沉鼎观收人，不看出身，不看荐书，只看三样：腿，脑子，胆子。」他把考牌翻过来，让执事看那三道，「三样，我这牌子上画满了。」他顿了一顿，没有看马小宝，只道，「最后那个名额，牌子上一个圈，一道是执事自己添的。」

殿里一下子静了。静了一会儿，队伍前头，孙二狗一声不吭，也把自己的考牌举了起来。跟着，殿角那个光脚的孩子也举了起来——他是不取的，举得比谁都高，牌子上三道，是他一试一试爬出来的。举牌子的只有这两个，别人都低着头。

执事的脸涨成了猪肝色，笔尖一转，指着小满喝道：「放肆！名额的事，轮得到你一个杂灵根来说？来人——」

笔尖离名册还有一寸，观主开了口：「慢。」他看了看测灵石，又看了看小满。他看小满的时候，比看测灵石的时候长得多，长得小满都有点发毛了。然后他转过头去，问靠在殿门口的那个人：「三试。瞿老以为如何？」

殿里的孩子们这才知道，那扫地的老头，原来是有名字的。瞿老拄着扫帚，只说了四个字：「腿稳。心细。」殿柱边上的几个老执事，互相看了一眼。瞿老在沉鼎观扫了五十年的台阶，四十多年没有收过一个徒弟；这四十多年里，他评孩子的话，统共评过不到三回，每回不超过两个字。

玄沉子点了点头：「收。外门。」执事的笔停在半空，道：「观主，名额——」玄沉子道：「添一个。」

执事张了张嘴，到底没说出什么来，低下头，在名册的末尾添了一行，又在那一行后头，添了两个小字：顶撞。然后挨个收新弟子的考牌。收到小满跟前，门口的瞿老道：「留着。」执事的手缩了回去。马小宝从小满身边走过去的时候，瞿老拿扫帚把门槛扫了一下，扫得很响。马小宝压低了声音，道：「沈小满，杂灵根也配进山门？等着。在这山里，我有的是法子收拾你。」小满道：「小宝哥，我等着。」

那天夜里，有个起夜的老弟子路过正殿，看见观主一个人坐在那口空石座旁边的蒲团上，也不打坐，也不念经，看着那口石座，一直坐到了三更。
story.en:
The spirit-testing stone lit — very dimly.

White-gold, green, black, red, yellow — five colours, not one missing, a little of each, none much, none bright, jostling one another, stirred together grey and murky, like a rag his mother had stitched from five kinds of leftover scraps. {主亮}

The hall went still for a moment.

Then someone laughed out loud. Loudest of all was Ma Xiaobao. He laughed till he rocked, laughed cake crumbs all over the floor, pointing at the testing stone as if at the joke of the century. With him laughing, the children in the hall all laughed, one catching it from the next, spreading patch by patch, the laughter hitting the faded beams and falling back down.

The name-calling steward smiled too, and drew it out as he read: "Metal, wood, water, fire, earth — all five elements. A false root with all five gates — the outer court calls it a mixed root. The lowest of the low." He lifted his brush. "The places are full. Not taken."

The brush tip came down toward the "not taken" column of the register. Xiaoman stood before the testing stone, his hand still on it, not taking it away. The three hundred steps he had climbed himself, the Luo diagram he had reckoned himself, the Longzhi's true head he had heard himself — and at the end of it, a stone, and a brush. He thought of his uncle sitting down on the hundred-and-sixtieth step for the length of a stick of incense; he thought of the torn jacket laid over something on the grass at the forest's edge. Of all the hall, laughing or staring, only two did not laugh: one was the abbot on his cushion; the other was Ah He. She stood at the back of the crowd, head down, and made a mark in her book with her charcoal, so hard the charcoal snapped.

Xiaoman ran a quick sum in his head: say nothing, and he's out; speak, and at worst he's out. He took his hand off the testing stone, took the trial tag from his jacket, and held it up. "Steward." The laughter in the hall thinned. He said: "This morning, the old man at the top of the stair said Chending Temple takes disciples not by birth, not by letters of recommendation, but by three things only: legs, head, nerve." He turned the tag so the steward could see the three strokes. "Three things — my tag's full." He paused, didn't look at Ma Xiaobao, and said only: "The last place — its tag has a circle on it, and one stroke the steward drew himself."

The hall went silent at once. After a moment, near the front of the line, Sun Ergou, without a word, held up his own tag. Then the barefoot boy in the corner held his up too — he was the one not taken, and he held it higher than anyone, three strokes on it, climbed one trial at a time. Only those two raised their tags; everyone else kept their heads down.

The steward's face went liver-red; he swung the brush tip round at Xiaoman and barked: "Insolence! Are the places the business of a mixed root? Someone —"

The brush tip an inch from the register, the abbot spoke: "Wait." He looked at the testing stone, then at Xiaoman. He looked at Xiaoman much longer than at the stone, so long Xiaoman's skin began to prickle. Then he turned and asked the man leaning in the doorway: "The three trials. What does Elder Qu think?"

Only then did the children in the hall learn that the old sweeper had a name. Elder Qu leaned on his broom and said just four words: "Steady legs. Careful heart." A few old stewards by the pillars exchanged a look. Elder Qu had swept the temple's stair for fifty years and taken no disciple in over forty; in those forty-odd years he had given a verdict on a child fewer than three times, never more than two words a time.

Xuanchenzi nodded. "Accepted. Outer court." The steward's brush hung in mid-air. "Abbot — the places —" Xuanchenzi said: "Add one."

The steward opened his mouth, said nothing in the end, lowered his head and added a line at the end of the register — and after that line, two small characters: *insubordinate*. Then he went along collecting the new disciples' trial tags. When he reached Xiaoman, Elder Qu in the doorway said: "Keep it." The steward's hand drew back. As Ma Xiaobao walked past Xiaoman, Elder Qu swept the threshold once with his broom, very loud. Ma Xiaobao said under his breath: "Shen Xiaoman, a mixed root, fit for the gate? You wait. On this mountain I've ways enough to deal with you." Xiaoman said, "Xiaobao-ge, are your trousers dry yet?" Ma Xiaobao opened his mouth to curse, choked on a mouthful of osmanthus cake, and coughed till his face went scarlet without coughing out a single word.

That night an old disciple, up in the night, passed the main hall and saw the abbot sitting alone on the cushion beside the empty stone stand, not meditating, not chanting, looking at the stand, until the third watch.
